Series::addmm¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::addmm(const Series& mat1, const Series& mat2,
              double beta = 1.0, double alpha = 1.0) const -> Series

What It Does¶

addmm() is the fused “bias plus matrix product” that a linear layer is built from:

addmm(input, mat1, mat2) = beta * input + alpha * (mat1 @ mat2)

mat1 is [m, k], mat2 is [k, n], and the receiver input broadcasts against the [m, n] product — usually it is the [n] bias row, or the full [m, n] accumulator. beta scales the existing input, alpha scales the new product; both default to 1.

It is exactly input.mul(beta).add(mat1.matmul(mat2).mul(alpha)), done as one call. The siblings pin the second factor’s shape:

method

product

second factor

addmm

matrix × matrix

[k, n]

addmv

matrix × vector

[k]

addr

outer product of two vectors

—

baddbmm

batched matrix × matrix

[b, k, n]

Reading The Three Roles¶

The receiver is not one of the multiplied matrices. In input.addmm(mat1, mat2), mat1 supplies rows, mat2 supplies columns, and input supplies an existing value to add to every output position. This is why a length-n receiver is useful: it is interpreted as one row and repeated over the m result rows by broadcasting.

Only the receiver broadcasts. mat1 and mat2 must both be matrices, and their shared k dimension must agree. Use matmul() when the factors themselves need batch broadcasting.

All three operands must also use the same dtype and platform. addmm() does not apply the general arithmetic promotion rules to a differently typed bias; convert it explicitly before the fused call.

Parameters¶

mat1 (const Series&) — the left factor, [m, k].

mat2 (const Series&) — the right factor, [k, n]. Its rows must match mat1’s columns.

beta (double, default 1.0) — scale on the existing input. beta = 0 drops input entirely (and skips reading it).

alpha (double, default 1.0) — scale on the mat1 @ mat2 product.

Returns¶

Series The [m, n] result beta * input + alpha * (mat1 @ mat2).

Gradient¶

addmm() is differentiable in input, mat1, and mat2. The backward is the standard matmul rule scaled by alpha, plus beta straight through to input:

d/d(input) = beta * g
d/d(mat1)  = alpha * (g @ mat2^T)
d/d(mat2)  = alpha * (mat1^T @ g)

When input was broadcast, its sensitivity is reduced back to the receiver’s original shape. For a row bias [n] used against an [m,n] result, that means summing the m output-row sensitivities. Setting beta=0 removes the receiver from both the forward value and its sensitivity and suppresses any NaN or infinity stored there.

Examples¶

Example 1. The default beta = alpha = 1: bias plus product.

auto bias = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 1.0}});
auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{5.0, 6.0}, {7.0, 8.0}});

std::cout << bias.addmm(a, b);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[20, 22],
  [43, 51]]

a @ b is [[19, 22], [43, 50]]; adding the identity bias gives the result.

Example 2. beta and alpha scale the two terms independently.

auto bias = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 1.0}});
auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{5.0, 6.0}, {7.0, 8.0}});

std::cout << bias.addmm(a, b, /*beta=*/0.5, /*alpha=*/2.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[38.5, 44],
  [86, 100.5]]

0.5 * bias + 2 * (a @ b).

Example 3. The gradient with respect to mat1.

auto bias = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 1.0}});
auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{5.0, 6.0}, {7.0, 8.0}});
a.tracks_slope_(true);

bias.addmm(a, b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "dL/da=" << a.sensitivity();

Output¶

dL/da=pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[11, 15],
  [11, 15]]

With g = ones(2, 2), dL/da = g @ b^T = [[1,1],[1,1]] @ [[5,7],[6,8]] = [[11,15],[11,15]].

Example 4. A row bias broadcasts over output rows.

auto bias = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0});
auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});
auto b = pluss::make_series({{5.0, 6.0}, {7.0, 8.0}});
std::cout << bias.addmm(a, b, 0.5, 2.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[43, 54],
  [91, 110]]

The product is [[19,22],[43,50]]; twice that product receives half of the bias row, [5,10], on each row.

Example 5. Inner dimensions that do not match are rejected.

auto bias = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 1.0}});
auto a = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {3.0, 4.0}});

try {
  bias.addmm(a, pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0, 3.0}}));
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n'));
}

Output¶

addmm: inner dimensions must match

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • mat1’s column count must equal mat2’s row count.

  • beta and alpha are plain scalars, not Series.

  • The receiver input broadcasts against [m, n]; a bias vector of length n is the common case.

  • Fully differentiable — this is the intended building block for a trainable linear map.

Summary¶

addmm(mat1, mat2, beta, alpha) fuses a scaled bias and a scaled matrix product:

  • beta * input + alpha * (mat1 @ mat2)

  • differentiable in all three tensors

  • vector / outer / batched variants: addmv, addr, baddbmm

  • Series::addmv / Series::addr / Series::baddbmm: the vector, outer-product, and batched forms.
